title: Athena Pay - Incident postmortem follow-up
summary: Follow-up on the 2026-03-02 outage affecting Athena Pay's payment validation flow. Discussed root cause (autoscaler headroom + routing policy mismatch), immediate mitigations applied, and longer-term reliability improvements. Agreed next steps: share full postmortem doc, run benchmarks, schedule rollout of autoscaler + routing policy changes in canary, and produce runbook and SLOs.
action_items: Priya Singh: Share full server logs, flame graphs and root-cause analysis doc by 2026-03-08
Alex Chen: Send pricing and options for Dedicated headroom (burst pool) and SLA add-on by 2026-03-06
Jordan Miles (Athena): Provide traffic pattern CSV and peak windows by 2026-03-07
Nora Liu (Athena): Confirm required audit log retention policy and KMS key ownership by 2026-03-10
Priya Singh: Draft runbook for similar incidents and share for review by 2026-03-12
Samir Rao: Schedule 2-hour canary rollout with Athena on 2026-03-15
next_steps: Redwood to share postmortem doc + diffs between v1 and fallback config
Athena to provide traffic traces and SLO targets
Schedule canary for autoscaler + routing policy changes
Agree on log retention and KMS integration approach
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 10:30 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Singh, Samir Rao (Redwood); Jordan Miles, Maya Patel, Luis Gomez, Nora Liu (Athena Pay)

[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining this follow up, i'll kick off quick and then priya will walk through the RCA details. um this is the postmortem followup from the outage on tuesday where your payment validation path saw ~25% errors and elevated latencies.

[00:22] Maya Patel: thanks Alex. appreciate you doing this. we had a bunch of exec questions, so want to make sure we cover root cause and timeline and what you changed already.

[00:35] Priya Singh: yep, quick tl;dr - root cause was twofold: first, the autoscaler had its headroom configured too tightly for the dedicated pool we were serving your validation model on; second, the smart-routing fallback didn't kick because the fallback model variant label didn't match the one used in the live routing policy (model variant metadata mismatch).

[01:05] Jordan Miles: right we saw a sudden traffic spike around 09:14 UTC, ~3x above typical 95th percentile, it coincided with a deploy on our side that increased batch sizes. autoscale did trigger but it was rate-limited and we hit queueing. requests sat in the front q and latencies spiked, then several timeouts.

[01:34] Priya Singh: correct, the autoscaler attempted to provision additional workers but our burst pool policy required a manual approval for certain instance types in the region; that delayed capacity by ~90s. also the fallback route was configured to a variant named v1a, but the live model was v1-a (dash vs no dash) - transcription/label mismatch, which prevented automatic fallback. small but important config mismatch.

[02:05] Luis Gomez: wow, the dash... that is painful. so you think the primary driver was provisioning headroom then the labeling prevented fallback?

[02:15] Priya Singh: yes, headroom first, labeling second. the headroom meant we had no graceful buffer so the tail latency explosion cascaded to error budgets.

[02:30] Maya Patel: what were the mitigations you did immediately?

[02:35] Alex Chen: right after we were alerted we applied three hotfixes: 1) we bumped autoscaler headroom to +40% for your dedicated pool, 2) we patched the routing policy to accept variant aliases (v1-a, v1a) so fallback can match, and 3) we increased KV cache retention for the validation prefix to reduce repeated cold starts. these were rolled in the control plane at ~09:48 UTC and we saw error rate normalize by ~10:02 UTC.

[03:05] Jordan Miles: error rate went back down, but we still had a few spikes until about 10:05. overall acceptable but execs want assurances this won't recur.

[03:18] Priya Singh: understood. longer-term proposals: (a) add automated pre-scaling based on scheduled deploys or detected batch-size changes, (b) add synthetics and stress tests against your validation path, (c) formalize fallback variant aliasing in the model catalog, (d) add circuit-breaker thresholds so we fail fast rather than queue up.

[03:52] Nora Liu: from security and compliance, we need stronger audit logs for model routing decisions and evidence that fallbacks occurred; also need KMS integration notes and SOC2 evidence for changes to the control plane.

[04:10] Alex Chen: we'll include audit log diffs and the KMS design doc in the postmortem. we have SOC2 artifacts but we'll point you to the relevant sections and add an appendix describing the change control around the hotfix.

[04:30] Maya Patel: can you quantify cost impact if we keep +40% headroom permanently? execs will want cost vs risk tradeoff.

[04:40] Alex Chen: yes priya will run a quick unit economics calc. rough estimate - +40% reserved headroom increases your monthly Dedicated commit utilization by ~28% on average for the validation pool; we can propose alternatives: scheduled headroom only during peak windows or dynamic burst with a cap and overage pricing. we'll send detailed pricing later.

[05:05] Priya Singh: also note Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization/profile changes for that model to reduce per-token compute - that would lower cost without increasing headroom. but we need a short eval to ensure quality doesn't degrade.

[05:25] Jordan Miles: ok makes sense. regarding the fallback aliasing - can you ensure changes are retroactive for existing models? we have older models in the catalog.

[05:35] Priya Singh: yes we plan a migration script that will add alias metadata for existing model entries; we'll run it in canary first.

[05:45] Luis Gomez: what about monitoring/alerts? our ops said the initial alert was triggered after the error rate had already spiked; can alerts be more sensitive?

[05:55] Samir Rao: we can tighten alert thresholds for your account; also add latency percentiles (p95/p99) on the route and anomaly detection on request patterns. we'll collaborate with you on thresholds.

[06:10] Maya Patel: are there any upstream vendor issues or infra provisioning delays on Redwood side that caused the 90s delay?

[06:20] Priya Singh: the 90s was mainly our policy around burst in that region - for that instance type we had an approval gate that required ops. we are automating that approval gate for standard customer burst in the next control-plane release. no external vendor outage.

[06:40] Jordan Miles: alright. execs will ask to see timeline and exact logs; can you provide a redacted log bundle?

[06:50] Alex Chen: yes we'll produce a redacted bundle and include timestamps, request ids, and flame graphs. Priya will attach a low-level RCA.

[07:05] Nora Liu: on KMS, Athena requires customer-managed keys for production. can Redwood support BYOK for these deployments?

[07:15] Priya Singh: yes our Private offering supports BYOK via standard KMS integrations; for Dedicated we can also support key ownership patterns - we'll detail options (bring-your-own-key vs Redwood-managed) in the follow-up.

[07:32] Maya Patel: timeline - when can we get the postmortem?

[07:36] Alex Chen: we'll aim for EOD Monday (2026-03-08) for the full postmortem and log bundle. pricing and headroom options by Friday (2026-03-06). a canary rollout scheduled for 2026-03-15, pending your sign-off.

[08:00] Jordan Miles: ok. can you also run a benchmark comparing current v1-a with the quantized variant you suggested? need latency and quality comparisons.
closing_notes: Meeting ended with recap of next steps, agreed dates for deliverables, and plan to run canary and benchmarks. Customer requested redacted logs, runbook, and cost scenarios. Redwood committed to postmortem doc by 2026-03-08.
